questions.question: Why can’t mathematical operations be directly applied to categorical / data?
questions.solution_html:
• Categorical data represents labels or categories, not numerical quantities. They do not have
  • inherent numeric value or order (no meaningful arithmetic relationship). Operations like
  • addition or subtraction do not provide meaningful results for categories. Categorical variables
  • are qualitative, so statistical/mathematical operations cannot interpret category differences
  • correctly. Any 2 points- (2 marks).
questions.final_answer: correctly. Any 2 points
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Why is data cleaning important in feature engineering?
questions.solution_html:
• Removes noise, errors, and inconsistencies from data to improve model performance. Ensures
  • high-quality and reliable features for accurate predictions. Helps handle missing values and
  • outliers that could mislead the model. Improves training efficiency and reduces bias in machine
  • learning models. Any two points- (2 Marks).
questions.final_answer: learning models. Any two points

questions.question: Why does normalization improve the performance of distance-based / algorithms?
questions.solution_html:
• Normalization scales all features to a similar range, preventing features with larger values from
  • dominating distance calculations. It ensures fair contribution of all features in algorithms like
  • KNN and K-Means. Helps the model converge faster and improves accuracy and stability of
  • results. Reduces the bias caused by varying units and magnitudes of features. Any two points
  • -(2 Marks)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What is handling missing data?
questions.solution_html:

  • values in a dataset. It ensures data quality and prevents skewed or incorrect results in analysis
  • or machine learning. Techniques include removal of missing entries, imputation, or using

questions.question: List the main steps in feature selection.
questions.solution_html:
• List the main steps in feature selection.
  • Identify relevant features from the dataset. Apply feature selection techniques (filter, wrapper
  • or embedded methods). Evaluate model performance with selected features. Remove
  • irrelevant, redundant, or highly correlated features. Any two points- (2 Marks).
questions.final_answer: irrelevant, redundant, or highly correlated features. Any two points
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Compare the practical advantages and limitations of filter, wrapper, and / hybrid feature selection methods with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Compare the practical advantages and limitations of filter wrapper and hybrid feature
  • selection methods with suitable examples.
  • Filter methods use statistical techniques to select features before applying any model.
  • Advantage: Fast and useful for high-dimensional datasets. . Limitation: Selection may not
  • always improve performance of a particular model since they ignore model behaviour.
  • Example: Correlation-based feature selection, Chi-square test. Wrapper Methods evaluate
  • subsets of features by training and testing a model repeatedly. Advantage: Produces features
  • specific to the model, improving accuracy. Limitation: Very slow and computationally
  • expensive; may leads to overfitting. Example: Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) with SVM
  • or Logistic Regression. Hybrid Methods combine filter and wrapper methods to balance speed
  • and accuracy. Advantage: More efficient than wrapper and more accurate than filter alone.
  • Limitation: More complex to design and implement. Example: Using a filter method to reduce
  • dimensionality first, then applying RFE. Any two points – (2 Marks).
questions.final_answer: dimensionality first, then applying RFE. Any two points
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain with examples how discrete data is different from continuous / data.
questions.solution_html:
• Definition of Discrete Data: Data that consists of distinct, separate values; countable; no
  • intermediate values possible (1 Mark).
  • Example of Discrete Data: Number of students in a class, number of cars, etc. (1 Mark).
  • Definition of Continuous Data: Data that can take any value within a range; measurable;
  • includes decimals/fractions (1 Mark).
  • Example of Continuous Data- Height, weight, temperature, stock prices, etc.(1 Mark).
  • Any one relevant comparison - Discrete → countable; Continuous → measurable, Discrete
  • values cannot be subdivided meaningfully; Continuous values can, Discrete shown as bar
  • graphs; continuous shown as histograms (1 Mark).
questions.final_answer: graphs; continuous shown as histograms
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss the importance of interaction features in real-world applications / (e.g., marketing, healthcare, finance). Provide at least two examples.
questions.solution_html:
• examples.
  • Definition / Meaning of Interaction Features: Interaction features capture combined effects of
  • two or more features that influence the target variable together. (1 Mark).
  • Importance in Real-World Applications (Any three valid points- (3 Marks) ). Helps discover
  • non-linear relationships between variables. Improves model accuracy and predictive power.
  • Reveals hidden patterns not captured by individual features. Essential in domains like
  • marketing, finance, medicine where combined influence matters. Reduces model bias by
  • including real-world variable interactions.
  • Any two examples such as: Marketing: Interaction of Income × Age to predict buying
  • behaviour, Healthcare: BP × Cholesterol interaction for heart disease risk, E-commerce
  • Discount × User Loyalty affecting purchase likelihood, Real Estate: Area × Location Rating
  • predicting house prices. (1 Mark).
questions.final_answer: predicting house prices
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of Label Encoding with / examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Compare the advantages and disadvantages of label encoding with examples.
  • Definition of Label Encoding. Converting categorical values into numeric labels (e.g., A → 0
  • B → 1). (2 Mark).
  • Advantages (Any Two- (1 Mark)) Simple and quick to implement. Useful for ordinal data where
  • order is important. Efficient storage and model processing due to numeric form.
  • Disadvantages (Any Two- (1 Mark)) Implies false ordinal relationships between categories. Can
  • mislead distance-based and tree-based models. Different numeric labels may affect model
  • output unintentionally.
  • Example with categories- (1 Mark): Example: Colors: Red, Blue, Green → 0, 1, 2 or Education
  • Level: High School → 0, UG → 1, PG → 2 (valid ordinal case)
questions.final_answer: Level: High School → 0, UG → 1, PG → 2 (valid ordinal case)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain with reasoning why PCA may reduce accuracy in classification / tasks.
questions.solution_html:
• PCA optimizes variance, not class separation-PCA finds orthogonal directions that capture the
  • most data variance. If class-distinguishing information lies in directions with low overall
  • variance, PCA may discard that information when you reduce dimensionality.
  • Discriminative signal may be low-variance.
  • Linear projection assumption. Standard PCA is linear. If classes are separable only by nonlinear
  • structure (manifold), PCA’s linear subspace projection will mix and collapse those nonlinear
  • distinctions.
  • Mixing of features reduces interpretability. Principal components are linear combinations of
  • original features. If a few original features were directly predictive, PCA spreads that
  • information across components; truncation can therefore lose the predictive contribution.
  • Scale and preprocessing sensitivity. If features aren’t properly scaled, PCA can emphasize
  • large-magnitude features regardless of their predictive power, harming classifiers that expect
  • balanced inputs.
  • Class imbalance and noise issues. Noise or a dominant majority class can drive variance
  • directions. PCA might then prioritize noise or majority-class variation, degrading performance
  • on minority classes. Any five valid points – (5 Marks)
questions.final_answer: on minority classes. Any five valid points
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
